c.tagline: Norway's fjord capital, where UNESCO wharves meet mountain funiculars.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are pricey and metered with higher night and weekend tariffs. Uber does not operate in Bergen, but Bolt is available; otherwise book by app, phone, or at ranks, as street-hailing is uncommon.

emergency.note: 112 reaches police, 113 ambulance, and 110 fire; 112 also works as the general EU-style emergency number.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed old Hanseatic wharf of leaning wooden merchant houses along the Vagen harbor; the historic heart best for first-timers who want landmarks, the fish market, and the Floibanen funicular all on foot.

The compact downtown core around Torgallmenningen, Ole Bulls plass, and Lille Lungegardsvann lake, packed with shops, restaurants, theaters, and hotels; the convenient central base for staying in the middle of everything.
A quiet residential peninsula of narrow lanes and white wooden houses reaching out to the aquarium and Nordnes park; calm and scenic, good for travelers who want seaside strolls and local atmosphere.

A historic district of preserved 18th-century wooden houses climbing the hillside north of the center along the fjord; peaceful and photogenic, suited to those wanting a residential, local feel near the water.
The university and student quarter around Nygardshoyden and the museum gardens, with cafes, bars, and cultural venues; an artsy, lively area popular with younger travelers and creatives.

landmarks: Bryggen
This UNESCO World Heritage wharf of colorful wooden Hanseatic buildings is the single most photographed sight in Norway.
Fløibanen (Mount Fløyen)
This funicular railway whisks visitors up Mount Fløyen for panoramic views over Bergen's harbor, fjords, and surrounding mountains.
Bergenhus Fortress
One of Norway's oldest and best-preserved fortresses, guarding the harbor entrance with centuries of royal and military history.
Rosenkrantz Tower
This medieval combined residence and defense tower within Bergenhus Fortress offers a striking silhouette and sweeping harbor views from its rooftop.
Fish Market (Fisketorget)
A lively waterfront market where fresh seafood, local color, and harbor backdrops make it a classic Bergen photo stop.
Bergen Cathedral
A striking stone church dating back to the 12th century, standing as one of the city's oldest and most storied buildings.
Ulriken (Ulriken643 Cable Car)
The highest of Bergen's seven mountains, reached by cable car, delivering the city's most expansive panoramic vistas.
Troldhaugen
Composer Edvard Grieg's lakeside villa and composing hut, a beautifully preserved cultural site set in tranquil natural surroundings.
KODE Art Museums
A cluster of art museums along Bergen's lake, home to major works by Edvard Munch and a hub of Norwegian cultural life.
St. Mary's Church (Mariakirken)
Bergen's oldest standing building, this twin-towered Romanesque church is a beautiful counterpoint to the nearby Bryggen wharf.

train.note: All trains use Bergen stasjon on Stromgaten, a short walk from the harbour and sharing a forecourt with the bus station. Vy's Bergensbanen runs several times daily to Oslo in about 6 hr 45 min plus a nightly sleeper, and the cheapest minipris fares are released roughly three months out on vy.no, so booking on the day is expensive. The Flam Railway connects at Myrdal and Vy sells a through-ticket covering both legs; if you are carrying a bicycle for the Rallarvegen you must add a bike ticket when you book. There are no international trains from Bergen at all - the nearest cross-border services to Sweden start from Oslo, so any rail trip abroad means riding the Bergen Line east first.

bus.note: Intercity coaches leave from Bergen busstasjon on Stromgaten, immediately beside the railway station. NOR-WAY Bussekspress runs the main network, including NW400 Kystbussen to Haugesund and Stavanger, NW180 Haukeliekspressen over the mountains to Oslo, NW420 Sognefjordekspressen to Sogndal and NW431 Fjordekspressen towards Forde and Nordfjord; buy at nor-way.no or in the app, and reservations are rarely essential outside holidays. Local and regional buses around the Bergen region are run separately by Skyss (https://www.skyss.no/). No scheduled international coach serves Bergen, so for Sweden, Denmark or the Continent you connect via Oslo.

intl.to: Kirkenes (Norway) - coastal voyage calling at 34 ports

ferry.note: Fjord Line uses Jekteviksterminalen, close enough to walk from the city centre, and its Hirtshals service runs year-round via Risavika in Stavanger; the crossing takes about 17.5 hours overnight, so a cabin or reclining Airseat is compulsory rather than optional. The same two ships, MS Stavangerfjord and MS Bergensfjord, cover the domestic Bergen to Stavanger leg in roughly 6.5 hours with no passport needed. Hurtigruten and Havila Voyages both sail the coastal route north to Kirkenes, calling at 34 ports over about six days each way; these are working coastal ships as well as cruises, so port-to-port tickets are sold alongside the full round trip. Norled's Sognefjord express boat to Flam runs roughly April to October and takes about 5.5 hours, and no ferry connects Bergen with the UK, Shetland or the Faroes any more.

half.name: Voss
half.blurb: A lake town in the mountains east of Bergen known as a base for extreme sports like paragliding, rafting, and skiing.

half.name: Mostraumen
half.blurb: A narrow, mountain-walled channel off the Osterfjord reached by boat cruise from Bergen, with waterfalls tumbling down sheer rock faces.

full.name: Hardangerfjord
full.blurb: Norway's second-longest fjord, lined with fruit orchards and waterfalls, and the starting point for the Trolltunga cliff hike.

full.name: Flåm
full.blurb: A fjord-side village reached partly by one of the world's steepest standard-gauge railways, descending to the Aurlandsfjord.
